title: Case Studies: Historical Exploits & Lessons
objectives: Reconstruct the Mango Markets $114M oracle manipulation on Solana
Reconstruct the Wormhole $325M signature verification bypass
Tell an economic design flaw apart from a code bug
See which defences modern protocols actually use

steps.title: Why We Study Exploits
steps.body:
Aviation is safe because every crash is investigated in public and the industry is forced to retrofit. DeFi learns the same way, only faster and with larger sums attached.

Hundreds of millions of dollars in historic exploits produced the safeguards you see today: confidence intervals on <Term id="oracle">oracles</Term>, isolated borrow markets, time-weighted prices, and stricter account checks in Solana programs. You cannot use those defences well unless you understand what they defend against.

steps.title: Case 1: The Mango Markets $114M Oracle Drain
steps.body:
October 2022, on Solana. The attacker funded two accounts with roughly $5M each and went to work on Mango Markets' perpetuals.

1. **The pump.** Account A took a massive short in MNGO-PERP while Account B took an equal long. MNGO was thinly traded, so aggressive buying on spot DEXs pushed the spot price from around $0.038 to about $0.91 within minutes.
2. **Paper profit as collateral.** Mango's risk engine marked Account B's unrealised position at over $400M and accepted that as valid <Term id="collateral">collateral</Term>.
3. **The drain.** The attacker borrowed $114M in real assets — SOL, USDC, BTC, mSOL — against that inflated mark, emptied the protocol's liquidity, and left behind bad debt.

No admin key was stolen and no contract was broken. The code did exactly what it was written to do: trust a manipulable spot price on an illiquid token. That is an economic design flaw, which is why an audit report alone would never have caught it.

steps.title: Case 2: The Wormhole $325M Signature Bypass
steps.body:
February 2022. Wormhole was Solana's largest cross-chain <Term id="bridge">bridge</Term>, and it lost about 120,000 wrapped ETH — roughly $325M at the time.

How bridges work, briefly: when you move ETH from Ethereum to Solana, a set of Guardian validators signs a message attesting that real ETH was deposited on the Ethereum side. Solana-side contracts verify those signatures before minting the wrapped token.

The flaw: Wormhole's Solana program relied on a system instruction to verify signatures, but it did not check that the account it read that instruction data from was the genuine sysvar account. The attacker supplied a spoofed account pre-loaded to look like a successful verification.

Result: the contract believed 120,000 ETH had been deposited and minted 120,000 wrapped ETH on Solana out of nothing.

Jump Crypto later topped up the bridge and the funds were largely recovered, but the lesson stayed: a bridge is only as strong as the smallest account-check in its verification path.

steps.title: Institutional Defenses: How Protocols Guard Today
steps.body:
Modern Solana protocols have built real defences against both attacks.

- **Pyth confidence intervals.** Pyth publishes not just a price but an uncertainty band around it. If a print spikes while the band is wide or market volume is thin, lending engines can reject the quote instead of pricing collateral with it.
- **Time-weighted average prices (TWAP).** Replaces volatile spot reads with multi-block averages, which makes a one-minute pump much more expensive to sustain.
- **Hard borrow caps.** Illiquid governance tokens either sit in isolated markets or carry strict global caps, so they cannot be used to borrow unlimited blue-chips.
- **Account constraint checks.** Anchor-style `#[account(address = sysvar::instructions::ID)]` constraints stop a program from accepting a spoofed sysvar — the exact class of bug that cost Wormhole $325M.

None of these are optional extras. They are the price of admission for a protocol that intends to hold other people's money.

steps.title: Under the Hood: Economic Exploit vs. Code Vulnerability
steps.body:
The two attacks differ in kind, and the difference is worth holding onto.

- **Wormhole was a code bug.** The verification pipeline accepted an account it should have rejected. The economics were irrelevant; the bug was in the plumbing.
- **Mango was an economic mechanism flaw.** Every line of code worked as written. The flaw was allowing an illiquid asset to serve as cross-margin collateral valued by a manipulable spot oracle.

The practical consequence: audit reports catch the first kind and routinely miss the second. When you look at a protocol, ask both questions — is the code written correctly, and is the design immune to someone playing it against itself? A protocol can be perfectly coded and still drainable.

questions.prompt: Why was the attacker in the Mango Markets exploit able to borrow $114M in real assets against an illiquid governance token?
options: They guessed the admin private key
They manipulated the spot oracle price on thin pools, and the protocol accepted the inflated paper profits as valid borrow collateral
They executed a 51% attack on the Solana validator network
The Mango program had a syntax compilation error
questions.explainRight: The attacker pumped a thin spot market, let the risk engine mark his perp position at that pumped price, then borrowed against the paper profit. Real assets left the protocol and worthless bad debt stayed behind. No key theft involved.
questions.explainWrong: There was no admin key, no 51% attack, and no compiler bug. The code did what it was written to do — trust a manipulable spot price on an illiquid asset when valuing collateral.

questions.prompt: How does Pyth Network's 'Confidence Interval' protect lending protocols from spot price manipulation?
options: It turns off the oracle whenever Bitcoin falls
It publishes an uncertainty band; if a price spikes abnormally without broad market volume, the wide confidence interval triggers safety freezes
It requires every user to pass KYC before borrowing
It automatically buys back dumped tokens with insurance reserves
questions.explainRight: Pyth reports a price together with an uncertainty band. When a print spikes with a wide band or thin volume, the lending engine treats the quote as unreliable and halts the borrow or liquidation that would have depended on it.
questions.explainWrong: No KYC and no automatic buybacks. The confidence interval measures how sure the oracle is, and wide uncertainty is a red flag a protocol can act on before it prices anything with it.

questions.prompt: What is the primary architectural rule modern lending protocols enforce to prevent the Mango Markets attack from recurring?
options: Allowing only 1 user per hour to borrow funds
Isolating illiquid tokens into separate pools and capping the amount that can ever be borrowed against them
Banning all perpetual contracts across DeFi
questions.explainRight: Isolate the risk. If an illiquid governance token can only borrow a capped amount in its own market, a 20x price pump cannot drain $114M of SOL and USDC from the main pool. Bad debt stays contained where it was created.
questions.explainWrong: Not rate limits on users, not banning USDC, not banning perps. Modern lending firewalls core assets by isolating volatile collateral and capping total borrowable exposure against it.
